Quandle Colorings of Knots and Applications

W. Edwin Clark    Mohamed Elhamdadi    Masahico Saito    Timothy Yeatman Affiliation: Department of Mathematics and Statistics Affiliation: University of South Florida
Abstract

We present a set of 26 finite quandles that distinguish (up to reversal and mirror image) by number of colorings, all of the 2977 prime oriented knots with up to 12 crossings. We also show that 1058 of these knots can be distinguished from their mirror images by the number of colorings by quandles from a certain set of 23 finite quandles. We study the colorings of these 2977 knots by all of the 431 connected quandles of order at most 35 found by L. Vendramin. Among other things, we collect information about quandles that have the same number of colorings for all of the 2977 knots. For example, we prove that if QQ is a simple quandle of prime power order then QQ and the dual quandle Q∗Q^{*} of QQ have the same number of colorings for all knots and conjecture that this holds for all Alexander quandles QQ. We study a knot invariant based on a quandle homomorphism f:Q1→Q0f:Q_{1}\rightarrow Q_{0}. We also apply the quandle colorings we have computed to obtain some new results for the bridge index, the Nakanishi index, the tunnel number, and the unknotting number. In an appendix we discuss various properties of the quandles in Vendramin’s list. Links to the data computed and various programs in C, GAP and Maple are provided.

Key words: Quandles, knot colorings, mirror images of knots, knot invariants.

1 Introduction

Sets with certain self-distributive operations called quandles have been studied since the 1940s in various areas with different names. They have been studied, for example, as algebraic systems for symmetries [45], as quasi-groups [18], and in relation to modules [21, 37]. Typical examples of quandles arise from conjugacy classes of groups and from modules over the integral Laurent polynomial ring ℤ⁡[t,t−1]\mathbb{Z}[t,t^{-1}], called Alexander quandles. The fundamental quandle of a knot was defined in a manner similar to the fundamental group [25, 32] of a knot, which made quandles an important tool in knot theory. The number of homomorphisms from the fundamental quandle to a fixed finite quandle has an interpretation as colorings of knot diagrams by quandle elements, and has been widely used as a knot invariant. Algebraic homology theories for quandles were defined [6, 17], and investigated in [29, 34, 38, 39, 40]. Extensions of quandles by cocycles have been studied [1, 5, 14], and invariants derived thereof are applied to various properties of knots and knotted surfaces (see [7] and references therein).

Tables of small quandles have been made previously (e.g., [7, 15, 37]). Computations using GAP by L. Vendramin [47] significantly expanded the list for connected quandles. He found all connected quandles of order up to 3535. There are 431431 of them. These quandles may be found in the GAP package RIG [46]. We refer to these quandles as RIG quandles, and use the notation C⁡[n,i]C[n,i] for the ii-th quandle of order nn in his list. As a matrix C⁡[n,i]C[n,i] is the transpose of the quandle matrix S​m​a​l​l​Q​u​a​n​d​l​e​(n,i)SmallQuandle(n,i) in [46].

In this paper, we investigate to what extent the number of quandle colorings of a knot by a finite quandle can distinguish the oriented knots with at most 12 crossings from the knot table at KnotInfo [8].

In Section 2, we provide definitions and conventions. The coloring of knots by quandles and the relationship to symmetry of knots are discussed in Section 3 and Section 4. It turns out that RIG quandles do not suffice to distinguish all of the prime, oriented knots with at most 12 crossings. To distinguish all of these knots we generated several thousand conjugation quandles and generalized Alexander quandles. Eventually we found a set of 2626 quandles that distinguish, up to orientation and mirror image, all knots with up to 1212 crossings. These computations extend the results by Dionisio and Lopes [12] for 1010 Alexander quandles and 249 prime knots with at most 10 crossings.

We write m⁡(K)m(K) for the mirror image of knot KK and r⁡(K)r(K) for KK with the orientation reversed. The 2977 knots given at KnotInfo [8] are representatives up to mirrors and reverses of the prime, oriented knots with at most 12 crossings (see [9]). It is known [30, 32] that quandle colorings do not distinguish KK from r​m​(K)rm(K) for any knot KK. Thus it is of interest which finite quandles, if any, can distinguish KK from m⁡(K)m(K). This is only possible for a knot which is chiral or negative amphicheiral. There are 1366 chiral or negative amphicheiral knots among the 2977 knots with up to 12 crossings at KnotInfo [8]. We have found a set of 2323 quandles that distinguish KK from m⁡(K)m(K) for 1058 knots out of these 1366 knots. It remains an open question whether the remaining 308 of these knots can be so distinguished.

Many sets of RIG quandles share the same number of colorings for all knots in the KnotInfo table. We explore this phenomenon in Section 5. For example, we conjecture that a connected Alexander quandle and its dual quandle always give the same number of colorings for any knot, and we prove this for a special class of Alexander quandles. In Section 6, we introduce an invariant of knots based on quandle homomorphisms and mention a relation to the quandle cocycle invariant. The computational results are applied to other knot invariants in Section 7, such as the bridge index, the Nakanishi index, the tunnel number and the unknotting number. Various properties of quandles are further discussed in Appendix A, and a summary of computational results is given as to these properties for RIG quandles. Descriptions of quandles used for distinguishing knots and their mirror images can be found in Appendix B. Files containing the quandle matrices, programs and the results of computations can be found at [48, 49]. Appendix C contains the list of 12 crossing knots discussed in Section 7. Appendix D contains some information on programs used for colorings.

2 Preliminaries

We briefly review some definitions and examples of quandles. More details can be found, for example, in [1, 7, 17].

A quandle XX is a set with a binary operation (a,b)↦a∗b(a,b)\mapsto a*b satisfying the following conditions.

(1) For any a∈Xa\in X, a∗a=aa*a=a.
(2) For any b,c∈Xb,c\in X, there is a unique a∈Xa\in X such that a∗b=ca*b=c.
(3) For any a,b,c∈Xa,b,c\in X, we have (a∗b)∗c=(a∗c)∗(b∗c).(a*b)*c=(a*c)*(b*c).

A quandle homomorphism between two quandles X,YX,Y is a map f:X→Yf:X\rightarrow Y such that f⁡(a∗Xb)=f⁡(a)∗Yf⁡(b)f(a*_{X}b)=f(a)*_{Y}f(b), where ∗X*_{X} and ∗Y*_{Y} denote the quandle operations of XX and YY, respectively. A quandle isomorphism is a bijective quandle homomorphism, and two quandles are isomorphic if there is a quandle isomorphism between them.

Typical examples of quandles include the following.

  • •

    Any non-empty set XX with the operation a∗b=aa*b=a for any a,b∈Xa,b\in X is a quandle called a trivial quandle.

  • •

    A conjugacy class XX of a group GG with the quandle operation a∗b=b−1​a​ba*b=b^{-1}ab. We call this a conjugation quandle.

  • •

    A generalized Alexander quandle is defined by a pair (G,f)(G,f) where GG is a group and f∈Aut⁡(G)f\in{\rm Aut}(G), and the quandle operation is defined by x∗y=f⁡(x​y−1)​yx*y=f(xy^{-1})y. If GG is abelian, this is called an Alexander quandle.

  • •

    A Galkin quandle is defined as follows. Let AA be an abelian group, also regarded naturally as a ℤ\mathbb{Z}-module. Let μ:ℤ3→ℤ\mu:\mathbb{Z}_{3}\rightarrow\mathbb{Z} , τ:ℤ3→A\tau:\mathbb{Z}_{3}\rightarrow A be functions. These functions μ\mu and τ\tau need not be homomorphisms. Define a binary operation on ℤ3×A\mathbb{Z}_{3}\times A by

    (x,a)∗(y,b)=(2​y−x,−a+μ⁡(x−y)​b+τ⁡(x−y))x,y∈ℤ3,a,b∈A.(x,a)*(y,b)=(2y-x,-a+\mu(x-y)b+\tau(x-y))\quad x,y\in\mathbb{Z}_{3},\ a,b\in A.

    Then for any abelian group AA, the above operation ∗* defines a quandle structure on ℤ3×A\mathbb{Z}_{3}\times A if μ⁡(0)=2\mu(0)=2, μ⁡(1)=μ⁡(2)=−1\mu(1)=\mu(2)=-1, and τ⁡(0)=0\tau(0)=0. Galkin gave this definition in [18], page 950950, for A=ℤpA=\mathbb{Z}_{p}, and this definition was given in [10].

  • •

    A function ϕ:X×X→A\phi:X\times X\rightarrow A for an abelian group AA is called a quandle 22-cocycle [6] if it satisfies

    ϕ⁡(x,y)−ϕ⁡(x,z)+ϕ⁡(x∗y,z)−ϕ⁡(x∗z,y∗z)=0\phi(x,y)-\phi(x,z)+\phi(x*y,z)-\phi(x*z,y*z)=0

    and ϕ⁡(x,x)=0\phi(x,x)=0 for any x,y,z∈Xx,y,z\in X. For a quandle 22-cocycle ϕ\phi, X×AX\times A becomes a quandle by (x,a)∗(y,b)=(x∗y,a+ϕ⁡(x,y))(x,a)*(y,b)=(x*y,a+\phi(x,y)) for x,y∈Xx,y\in X, a,b∈Aa,b\in A, and it is called an abelian extension of XX by AA, see [5].

Let XX be a quandle. The right translation ℛa:X→X{\cal R}_{a}:X\rightarrow X, by a∈Xa\in X, is defined by ℛa​(x)=x∗a{\cal R}_{a}(x)=x*a for x∈Xx\in X. Similarly the left translation ℒa{\cal L}_{a} is defined by ℒa​(x)=a∗x{\cal L}_{a}(x)=a*x. Then ℛa{\cal R}_{a} is a permutation of XX by Axiom (2). The subgroup of Sym⁡(X){\rm Sym}(X) generated by the permutations ℛa{\cal R}_{a}, a∈Xa\in X, is called the inner automorphism group of XX, and is denoted by Inn⁡(X){\rm Inn}(X). A quandle is connected if Inn⁡(X){\rm Inn}(X) acts transitively on XX. The operation ∗¯\bar{*} on XX defined by a​∗¯​b=ℛb−1​(a)a\ \bar{*}\ b={\cal R}_{b}^{-1}(a) is a quandle operation, and (X,∗¯)(X,\bar{*}) is called the dual quandle of (X,∗)(X,*). We also denote the dual of XX by X∗X^{*}. If X∗X^{*} is isomorphic to XX, then XX is called self-dual.

We write K=K′K=K^{\prime} to denote that there is an orientation preserving homeomorphism of 𝕊3\mathbb{S}^{3} that takes KK to K′K^{\prime} preserving the orientations of KK and K′K^{\prime}. A coloring of an oriented knot diagram by a quandle XX is a map 𝒞:𝒜→X{\cal C}:{\cal A}\rightarrow X from the set of arcs 𝒜{\cal A} of the diagram to XX such that the image of the map satisfies the relation depicted in Figure 2 at each crossing. More details can be found in [7, 13], for example. A coloring that assigns the same element of XX to all the arcs is called trivial, otherwise non-trivial. The number of colorings of a knot diagram by a finite quandle is known to be independent of the choice of a diagram, and hence is a knot invariant. In Figure 2, a coloring of a figure-eight knot is indicated. In the figure, the elements x,y,zx,y,z of a quandle are assigned at the top arcs. The coloring conditions are applied to color other arcs as depicted. Since the bottom arcs are connected to the top arcs, we need the conditions

x\displaystyle x =\displaystyle= z​∗¯​(x∗y),\displaystyle z\ \overline{*}\ (x*y),
y\displaystyle y =\displaystyle= (x∗y)​∗¯​(y∗(z​∗¯​(x∗y))),\displaystyle(x*y)\ \overline{*}\ (y*(z\ \overline{*}\ (x*y))),
z\displaystyle z =\displaystyle= y∗(z​∗¯​(x∗y)).\displaystyle y*(z\ \overline{*}\ (x*y)).

to obtain a coloring. Each crossing corresponds to a standard generator σi\sigma_{i} of the 33-strand braid group or its inverse, and the closure of σ1​σ2−1​σ1​σ2−1\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2}^{-1}\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2}^{-1} represents the figure-eight knot. The dotted lines indicate the closure, see [44] for more details on braids. We give the orientation downward for braids, see the figure. For the rest of this paper all knots will be prime and oriented.

The fundamental quandle is defined in a manner similar to the fundamental group [25, 32]. A presentation of a quandle is defined in a manner similar to groups as well, and a presentation of the fundamental quandle is obtained from a knot diagram (see, for example, [16]), by assigning generators to arcs of a knot diagram, and relations corresponding to crossings. The set of colorings of a knot diagram KK by a quandle XX, then, is in one-to-one correspondence with the set of quandle homomorphisms from the fundamental quandle of KK to XX.

If QQ is a quandle and KK is a knot we denote by ColQN​(K){\rm Col}^{N}_{Q}{(K)} the number of non-trivial colorings of KK by QQ. The number of colorings including trivial colorings is ColQ​(K)=ColQN​(K)+|Q|{\rm Col}_{Q}{(K)}={\rm Col}^{N}_{Q}{(K)}+|Q|, where |Q||Q| is the order of QQ. It is well known that for each quandle Q, ColQ​(K){\rm Col}_{Q}{(K)} is an invariant of knots ([43], for example). We say that the quandle QQ distinguishes knots KK and K′K^{\prime} if ColQ​(K)≠ColQ​(K′){\rm Col}_{Q}{(K)}\neq{\rm Col}_{Q}{(K^{\prime})}.

Let m:𝕊3→𝕊3m:\mathbb{S}^{3}\rightarrow\mathbb{S}^{3} be an orientation reversing homeomorphism. For a knot KK, m⁡(K)m(K) is the mirror image of KK. Let r⁡(K)r(K) denote the same knot KK with its orientation reversed. We regard mm and rr as maps on equivalence classes of knots. We consider the group 𝒢={1,r,m,r​m}\mathcal{G}=\{1,r,m,rm\} acting on the set of all oriented knots. For each knot KK let 𝒢⁡(K)={K,r⁡(K),m⁡(K),r​m​(K)}\mathcal{G}(K)=\{K,r(K),m(K),rm(K)\} be the orbit of KK under the action of 𝒢\mathcal{G}.

By a symmetry we mean that a knot (type) KK remains unchanged under one of rr, mm, r​mrm. As in the definition of symmetry type in [8] we say that a knot KK is

  • •

    reversible if the only symmetry it has is K=r⁡(K)K=r(K),

  • •

    negative amphicheiral if the only symmetry it has is K=r​m​(K)K=rm(K) ,

  • •

    positive amphicheiral if the only symmetry it has is K=m⁡(K)K=m(K),

  • •

    chiral if it has none of these symmetries,

  • •

    fully amphicheiral if it has all three symmetries, that is, K=r⁡(K)=m⁡(K)=r​m​(K)K=r(K)=m(K)=rm(K).

The symmetry type of each knot on at most 12 crossings is given at [8]. Thus each of the 29772977 knots KK given there represents as many as four knots K,m⁡(K),r⁡(K)K,m(K),r(K) and r​m​(K)rm(K).

It is known [30, 32] that the fundamental quandles of KK and K′K^{\prime} are isomorphic if and only if K=K′K=K^{\prime} or K=r​m​(K′)K=rm(K^{\prime}).

3 Distinguishing the knots K,m⁡(K),r⁡(K),r​m​(K)K,m(K),r(K),rm(K)

For the problem of distinguishing knots by quandle coloring it suffices to consider only connected quandles by the following lemma (see Ohtsuki [41], Section 5.2).

Lemma 3.1

The image of a quandle homomorphism of the fundamental quandle of any knot in another quandle is connected. In particular, given two knots K1K_{1} and K2K_{2}, a quandle QQ of smallest order satisfying ColQ​(K1)≠ColQ​(K2){\rm Col}_{Q}{(K_{1})}\neq{\rm Col}_{Q}{(K_{2})} is connected.

Lemma 3.2

The following equations hold for all quandles QQ and all knots KK:

  • (1)(1)

    ColQ​(K)=ColQ​(r​m​(K)){\rm Col}_{Q}{(K)}={\rm Col}_{Q}{(rm(K))},

  • (2)(2)

    OPENOPENColQ​(r⁡(K)))=ColQ​(m⁡(K))){\rm Col}_{Q}{(r(K)))}={\rm Col}_{Q}{(m(K)))},

  • (3)(3)

    ColQ​(m⁡(K))=ColQ∗​(K){\rm Col}_{Q}{(m(K))}={\rm Col}_{Q^{*}}{(K)},

where Q∗Q^{*} in (3)(3) denotes the dual quandle of QQ.

Proof: For (1) and (2) see Kamada [26]. Item (3) follows easily from the definitions.  

Corollary 3.3

For all quandles QQ and for knots KK of any symmetry type except chiral or negative amphicheiral,

ColQ​(r​m​(K))=ColQ​(m⁡(K))=ColQ​(r⁡(K))=ColQ​(K).{\rm Col}_{Q}{(rm(K))}={\rm Col}_{Q}{(m(K))}={\rm Col}_{Q}{(r(K))}={\rm Col}_{Q}{(K)}.

There exists a sequence of finite quandles 𝒮=(Q1,Q2,…,Qn,…)\mathcal{S}=(Q_{1},Q_{2},\ldots,Q_{n},\ldots) such that the invariant

This proves the first part of the proposition. Now assume that (A), (B), (C), (D) hold and K∼K′K\sim K^{\prime}. Let kk and k′k^{\prime} be as above. By what we just proved we have 𝒢⁡(k)=𝒢⁡(k′)\mathcal{G}(k)=\mathcal{G}(k^{\prime}) and so we have K,K′∈𝒢⁡(k)K,K^{\prime}\in\mathcal{G}(k). If K=K′K=K^{\prime} there is nothing to prove so we can assume that one of the following 4 cases holds and that K≠K′K\neq K^{\prime}.

  • Case(1)

    kk is reversible or positive amphicheiral. Hence 𝒢⁡(k)={k,r​m​(k)}\mathcal{G}(k)=\{k,rm(k)\}. In this case we may take K=kK=k and K′=r​m​(k)K^{\prime}=rm(k) so K′=r​m​(K)K^{\prime}=rm(K).

  • Case(2)

    kk is negative amphicheiral. Hence 𝒢⁡(k)={k,m⁡(k)}\mathcal{G}(k)=\{k,m(k)\}. In this case by (D) we have that k≁m⁡(k)k\nsim m(k) so K≠K′K\neq K^{\prime}, K∼K′K\sim K^{\prime} and K,K′∈𝒢⁡(k)K,K^{\prime}\in\mathcal{G}(k) is impossible.

  • Case(3)

    kk is chiral. Hence 𝒢⁡(k)={k,r⁡(k),m⁡(k),r​m​(k)}\mathcal{G}(k)=\{k,r(k),m(k),rm(k)\}. Of the four elements of 𝒢⁡(k)\mathcal{G}(k) there are 6 possible pairs that might be {K,K′}\{K,K^{\prime}\}. Note that the pair {k,m⁡(k)}\{k,m(k)\} is ruled out by (D). Since we always have k∼r​m​(k)k\sim rm(k) and r⁡(k)∼m⁡(k)r(k)\sim m(k), the pairs {k,r⁡(k)}\{k,r(k)\}, {r​m​(k),m⁡(k)}\{rm(k),m(k)\}, {r​m​(k),r⁡(k)}\{rm(k),r(k)\}, are also ruled out. This leaves the only possibilities to be {k,r​m​(k)}\{k,rm(k)\} and {r⁡(k),r​m​(k)}\{r(k),rm(k)\}. If r⁡(k)∼r​m​(k)r(k)\sim rm(k) then m⁡(k)∼r⁡(k)∼r​m​(k)∼km(k)\sim r(k)\sim rm(k)\sim k which is a contradiction to (D), so we are left with {k,r​m​(k)}\{k,rm(k)\} as the only possibility for {K,K′}\{K,K^{\prime}\}, as desired.

  • Case(4)

    kk is fully amphicheiral. Hence 𝒢⁡(k)={k}\mathcal{G}(k)=\{k\}. This is impossible since there is only a single knot in 𝒢⁡(k)\mathcal{G}(k).

This completes the proof.  

4 Computational support for Conjectures 3.4 and 3.5

Let 𝒬26=(Q1,…,Q26)\mathcal{Q}_{26}=(Q_{1},\ldots,Q_{26}) be the list of 26 quandles in Table B.1 in Appendix B. Matrices for these 26 quandles may be found at [48], where they are denoted by Q⁡[i],i=1,…,26Q[i],i=1,\ldots,26. The list 𝒬26\mathcal{Q}_{26} is closed under taking dual quandles. This is to simplify computing the number of colorings of the mirror image of a knot. Included in the file is the list dual satisfying d​u​a​l​[i]=jdual[i]=j if and only if Qi∗Q_{i}^{*} is isomorphic to Qj.Q_{j}.

If i≠15i\neq 15 each quandle QiQ_{i} is faithful and hence isomorphic to a conjugation quandle on some conjugacy class in its inner automorphism group Inn(QiQ_{i}). The quandle Q15Q_{15} is not faithful and is not a conjugation quandle [Vendramin, personal communication]. We note that some non-faithful quandles are conjugation quandles, so this is not trivial. However, Q15Q_{15} is a generalized Alexander quandle on GAP’s SmallGroup(32,50)=(C​2×Q​8):C​2(32,50)=(C2\times Q8):C2. The quandles in 𝒬26{\mathcal{Q}}_{26} of order less than 36 are RIG quandles and the remaining 11 were found by searching for conjugation quandles on conjugacy classes of finite groups using GAP. In retrospect all of these 26 quandles could have been found by searching for conjugation quandles and generalized Alexander quandles.

We denote the knots in KnotInfo up to 12 crossings by

ℛ12={K[i]:i=1,…,2977}.\mathcal{R}_{12}=\{K[i]:i=1,\ldots,2977\}.

In our notation, the knot K⁡[i]K[i] represents the knot with name rank =i+1=i+1 in [8]. In particular, K⁡[1]K[1] is the trefoil, which has name rank 22 in [8].

The 26×297726\times 2977 matrix MM found at [48] has the property that

Mi,j=ColQiN​(K⁡[j]).M_{i,j}={\rm Col}^{N}_{Q_{i}}{(K[j])}.

See Appendix D for comments on the computation of ColQN​(K){\rm Col}^{N}_{Q}{(K)}.

Since ℛ12\mathcal{R}_{12} is a set of representatives of the set 𝒦12\mathcal{K}_{12} of (isotopy classes of prime, oriented) knots with at most 1212 crossings, including all symmetry types, to verify that Conjecture 3.4 holds when 𝒦=𝒦12\mathcal{K}=\mathcal{K}_{12} and the list of quandles 𝒮=𝒬26\mathcal{S}=\mathcal{Q}_{26}, it suffices, by Proposition 3.7, to verify that the matrix MM and the list d​u​a​ldual has the following properties for i,j∈{1,2,…,2977}i,j\in\{1,2,\ldots,2977\} and k∈{1,2,…,26}k\in\{1,2,\ldots,26\}.

  • (1)(1)

    For all i≠ji\neq j there exists kk such that Mk,i≠Mk,jM_{k,i}\neq M_{k,j}.

  • (2)(2)

    For all i≠ji\neq j there exists kk such that Mk,i≠Ms,jM_{k,i}\neq M_{s,j}, where s=d​u​a​l​[k]s=dual[k].

  • (3)(3)

    For all i≠ji\neq j there exists kk such that Ms,i≠Ms,jM_{s,i}\neq M_{s,j}, where s=d​u​a​l​[k]s=dual[k].

These conditions are easy to verify directly from the matrix MM and the list d​u​a​ldual. This shows that the set 𝒬26\mathcal{Q}_{26} distinguishes the knots in 𝒦12\mathcal{K}_{12} up to mirror images and orientation.

Remark 4.1

Note that the unknot is not included among the knots K[i], i=1,…,2977i=1,\ldots,2977. Since the unknot has only trivial colorings, to show that we can distinguish it from all of the 2977 knots it suffices to note that for every knot K⁡[j]K[j] there is a quandle QiQ_{i} such that ColQiN​(K⁡[j])≠0{\rm Col}^{N}_{Q_{i}}{(K[j])}\neq 0, that is, no column of the matrix M contains only 00s. This is confirmed from the matrix MM.

As pointed out above the only knots we can hope to distinguish from their mirror images (equivalently from their reversals) are chiral knots and negative amphicheiral knots. Among 2977 knots in KnotInfo [8] up to 12 crossings, 1319 knots are chiral and 47 are negative amphicheiral. Denote this set of 1366 knots by 𝒦c\mathcal{K}^{c}. We were not able to find quandles to distinguish all of these 1366 knots from their mirror images. Thus we cannot verify Conjecture 3.5 when 𝒦=𝒦12\mathcal{K}=\mathcal{K}_{12}. However, were able to find quandles that distinguish 1058 of the knots in 𝒦c\mathcal{K}^{c} from their mirror images. The quandles that distinguish these 1058 knots are the quandles T1,T2,…,T23T_{1},T_{2},\ldots,T_{23} in Table B.2. Matrices for the quandles can be found in [48]. A list of 1058 pairs (i,n)(i,n) where K⁡[n]K[n] is one of 1058 knots in 𝒦c\mathcal{K}^{c} and TiT_{i} is a quandle that distinguished knot K⁡[n]K[n] from m⁡(K⁡[n])m(K[n]) can be found in [48].

With the exception of quandles T2T_{2} and T3T_{3} the quandles TiT_{i} are conjugation quandles on conjugation classes in the group I​n​n​(Ti)Inn(T_{i}). T2T_{2} and T3T_{3} are generalized Alexander quandles, both on the group P​S​L​(2,8)PSL(2,8). We note that Q17=T22Q_{17}=T_{22} and Q24=T23Q_{24}=T_{23}. Otherwise the quandles in Table B.2 are different from those in Table B.1

In Table B.1 and Table B.2 the structure descriptions are given by GAP’s StructureDescription function. In particular, A×BA\times B is the direct product, N:HN:H is a semidirect product and A.BA.B is a non-split extension. The group ID, S​m​a​l​l​G​r​o​u​p​(n,i)SmallGroup(n,i) is the iith group of order nn in the GAP Small Groups library for nn at most 2000. If a group has order n>2000n>2000 we write S​m​a​l​l​G​r​o​u​p​(n,0)SmallGroup(n,0). Nevertheless for all of the inner automorphism groups we have computed, GAP does give a Structure Description.

5 Similarity of quandles over knot colorings

For two quandles Q1Q_{1} and Q2Q_{2}, and a set 𝒦{\mathcal{K}} of knots, we write Q1≈𝒦Q2Q_{1}\approx_{\mathcal{K}}Q_{2} if ColQ1​(K)=ColQ2​(K){\rm Col}_{Q_{1}}{(K)}={\rm Col}_{Q_{2}}{(K)} for all K∈𝒦K\in{\mathcal{K}}.

This equivalence relation was considered in [10]. We omit the subscript 𝒦{\mathcal{K}} when it is the set of all knots. The following is immediate from the definitions and a property of the number of colorings.

Lemma 5.1

If Q1≈Q1′Q_{1}\approx Q_{1}^{\prime} and Q2≈Q2′Q_{2}\approx Q_{2}^{\prime} then (Q1×Q2)≈(Q1′×Q2′)(Q_{1}\times Q_{2})\approx(Q_{1}^{\prime}\times Q_{2}^{\prime}).

Let 𝒦{\mathcal{K}} be the set of all 29772977 knots in the table in KnotInfo [8] up to 1212 crossings. We observe the following for ≈𝒦\approx_{\mathcal{K}} and for the 431 RIG quandles.

  • •

    There are 151151 classes of ≈𝒦\approx_{\mathcal{K}} consisting of more than one quandle.

  • •

    Among these classes, 145145 classes consist of two quandles.

  • •

    Among 145145 classes of pairs, all but 3535 classes consist of a pair of dual Alexander quandles.

  • •

    Among 3535 classes of pairs, one class is a pair of self-dual Alexander quandles, some are non-Alexander dual quandles, and some are non-Alexander self-dual quandles.

Conjecture 5.2

For every connected Alexander quandle QQ, Q≈Q∗Q\approx Q^{*}.

We prove the above conjecture for simple Alexander quandles of prime power order. (Following [1] we say that a quandle QQ is simple if it is not trivial and whenever f:Q→Q′f:Q\rightarrow Q^{\prime} is an epimorphism then ff is an isomorphism or |Q′|=1|Q^{\prime}|=1. This implies that |Q|>2|Q|>2 since the quandles of orders 1 and 2 are trivial.) The following proposition gives alternative characterizations of these quandles.

Proposition 5.3

The following statements are equivalent for a quandle QQ and a prime pp.

  • (1)

    QQ is a simple quandle with pkp^{k} elements.

  • (2)

    QQ is isomorphic to an Alexander quandle on ℤp​[t,t−1]/(h⁡(t))\mathbb{Z}_{p}[t,t^{-1}]/(h(t)) where h​(t)∈ℤp​[t]h(t)\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}[t] is irreducible, of degree kk and different from tt and t−1t-1 and the quandle operation is defined by x∗y=t¯​x+(1−t¯)​yx*y=\overline{t}x+(1-\overline{t})y where t¯\overline{t} is the coset t+(h⁡(t))t+(h(t)).

  • (3)

    QQ is isomorphic to an Alexander quandle on the vector space (𝔽p)k{(\mathbb{F}_{p})}^{k} where TT is the companion matrix of a monic irreducible polynomial h​(t)∈ℤp​[t]h(t)\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}[t] of degree kk, different from tt and t−1t-1 and the quandle operation is given by x∗y=T​x+(1−T)​yx*y=Tx+(1-T)y.

  • (4)

    QQ is isomorphic to a quandle defined on the finite field 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} where q=pkq=p^{k}, a∈𝔽qa\in\mathbb{F}_{q}, a≠1a\neq 1, aa generates 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}, and the quandle operation is given by x∗y=a​x+(1−a)​yx*y=ax+(1-a)y for x,y∈𝔽qx,y\in\mathbb{F}_{q}.

Proof. The equivalence of (1), (3) and (4) is proved in [1] Section 3. The equivalence of (2) and (4) is proved in [2]. □\Box

Proposition 5.4

If QQ is a simple quandle of prime power order, then Q≈Q∗Q\approx Q^{*}.

Proof. By Proposition 5.3, the quandle QQ is equal to (𝔽q,∗)(\mathbb{F}_{q},*) where 𝔽q=ℤp​[t,t−1]/(h⁡(t))\mathbb{F}_{q}=\mathbb{Z}_{p}[t,t^{-1}]/(h(t)), q=pkq=p^{k}, h​(t)∈ℤp​[t]h(t)\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}[t] is irreducible of degree kk. The quandle operation is defined by x∗y=t¯​x+(1−t¯)​yx*y=\overline{t}x+(1-\overline{t})y where t¯\overline{t} is the coset t+(h⁡(t))t+(h(t)). Let S∈Mn​(𝔽q)S\in M_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q}) denote the reduction modulo (p,h⁡(t))(p,h(t)) of a Seifert matrix of KK, and let N=t¯​S−STN=\overline{t}S-S^{T}, which is denoted by N⁡(1,p,h⁡(t))N(1,p,h(t)) in [2]. Although pp is restricted to odd primes in [2], we claim that their results hold for p=2p=2 also. The authors of [2] agree (personal communication).

Let φ:𝔽qn→𝔽qn\varphi:\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n} be the linear map that NN represents. Then in [2] it was shown that the set of colorings SColQ​(K){\rm SCol}_{Q}{(K)} is in one-to-one correspondence with the module 𝔽q⊕ker⁡(φ)\mathbb{F}_{q}\oplus{\rm ker}(\varphi).

The dual quandle Q∗Q^{*} is equal to (𝔽q,∗¯)(\mathbb{F}_{q},\overline{*}) where a​∗¯​b=t¯−1​a+(1−t¯−1)​ba\ \overline{*}\ b={\overline{t}}^{-1}a+(1-{\overline{t}}^{-1})b. Let N∗=t¯−1​S−STN^{*}=\overline{t}^{-1}S-S^{T}, and φ∗:𝔽qn→𝔽qn\varphi^{*}:\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n} be the corresponding linear map. Then the number of colorings by Q∗Q^{*} is the cardinality of 𝔽q⊕ker⁡(φ∗)\mathbb{F}_{q}\oplus{\rm ker}(\varphi^{*}). It remains to show that the dimensions of ker⁡(φ){\rm ker}(\varphi) and ker⁡(φ∗){\rm ker}(\varphi^{*}) are the same. One computes

(−t¯−1)​NT=−t¯−1​(t¯​ST−S)=−ST+t¯−1​S=N∗.(-\overline{t}^{-1})N^{T}=-\overline{t}^{-1}(\overline{t}S^{T}-S)=-S^{T}+\overline{t}^{-1}S=N^{*}.

Since rank⁡(NT)=rank⁡(N){\rm rank}(N^{T})={\rm rank}(N), we have rank⁡(N)=rank⁡(N∗){\rm rank}(N)={\rm rank}(N^{*}) and hence the dimension of the kernel of φ∗\varphi^{*} is equal to the dimension of the kernel of φ\varphi, so the number of colorings is the same for QQ and Q∗Q^{*}. □\Box

This proof is similar to the proof of the fact that the Alexander polynomial is symmetric, Δ⁡(t−1)=Δ⁡(t)\Delta(t^{-1})=\Delta(t) modulo a power of tt.

From Proposition 5.4 and Lemma 5.1 we obtain the following corollary.

Corollary 5.5

If a quandle QQ is isomorphic to a product of simple quandles of prime power order then Q≈Q∗Q\approx Q^{*}.

There are 273 connected Alexander quandles of order at most 35. Only 45 of these quandles are not a product of simple quandles of prime power order.

6 Quandle homomorphisms and knot colorings

We write SColQ​(K){\rm SCol}_{Q}{(K)} to denote the set of all colorings of the knot KK by the quandle QQ.

Let f:Q1→Q0f:Q_{1}\rightarrow Q_{0} be a quandle homomorphism, and KK be a knot. Note that for any coloring y∈SColQ1​(K)y\in{\rm SCol}_{Q_{1}}{(K)} regarded as a quandle homomorphism Q⁡(K)→Q1Q(K)\rightarrow Q_{1}, the composition x=f∘y:Q⁡(K)→Q0x=f\circ y:Q(K)\rightarrow Q_{0} is a coloring in SColQ0​(K){\rm SCol}_{Q_{0}}{(K)}. In this case we say that xx lifts to yy. This correspondence defines a map f♯:SColQ1​(K)→SColQ0​(K)f_{\sharp}:{\rm SCol}_{Q_{1}}{(K)}\rightarrow{\rm SCol}_{Q_{0}}{(K)}.

For x∈SColQ0​(K)x\in{\rm SCol}_{Q_{0}}{(K)}, denote by f♯−1​(x)⊂SColQ1​(K)f_{\sharp}^{-1}(x)\subset{\rm SCol}_{Q_{1}}{(K)} the set of colorings y∈SColQ1​(K)y\in{\rm SCol}_{Q_{1}}{(K)} such that f♯​(y)=xf_{\sharp}(y)=x. (This set may be empty.) A pair of colorings x∈SColQ0​(K)x\in{\rm SCol}_{Q_{0}}{(K)} and y∈SColQ1​(K)y\in{\rm SCol}_{Q_{1}}{(K)} such that x=f∘yx=f\circ y for a knot diagram determines another such a pair after each Reidemeister move, and hence for each x∈SColQ0​(K)x\in{\rm SCol}_{Q_{0}}{(K)}, the cardinality |f♯−1​(x)||f_{\sharp}^{-1}(x)| does not depend on the choice of diagrams. Thus we obtain the following knot invariant.

Definition 6.1

For a given quandle homomorphism f:Q1→Q0f:Q_{1}\rightarrow Q_{0}, we denote by Colf​(K){\rm Col}_{f}(K) the multiset {|f♯−1​(x)||x∈SColQ0​(K)}\{|f_{\sharp}^{-1}(x)|\ |\ x\in{\rm SCol}_{Q_{0}}{(K)}\}, that does not depend on the choice of a diagram of a knot.

We use the notation [a,k][a,k] for kk copies of the element aa. For example, {[0,3],[2,4]}\{[0,3],[2,4]\} represents {0,0,0,2,2,2,2}\{0,0,0,2,2,2,2\}. We observe the following.

  • •

    If Colf​(K)={[h1,k1],…,[hn,kn]}{\rm Col}_{f}(K)=\{[h_{1},k_{1}],\ldots,[h_{n},k_{n}]\}, then ColQ0​(K)=k1+⋯+kn{\rm Col}_{Q_{0}}{(K)}=k_{1}+\cdots+k_{n} and ColQ1​(K)=h1​k1+⋯+hn​kn{\rm Col}_{Q_{1}}{(K)}=h_{1}k_{1}+\cdots+h_{n}k_{n}.

  • •

    Suppose Q1Q_{1} is connected. If ColQ0N​(K)=0{\rm Col}^{N}_{Q_{0}}{(K)}=0 (i.e. KK is only trivially colored by Q0Q_{0}) and ff is an epimorphism, then Colf​(K)={[h,k]}{\rm Col}_{f}(K)=\{[h,k]\}, where k=|Q0|k=|Q_{0}| and h=ColQ1​(K)/|Q0|h={\rm Col}_{Q_{1}}{(K)}/|Q_{0}|.

  • •

    Suppose Q1Q_{1} is connected. If ColQ1N​(K)=0{\rm Col}^{N}_{Q_{1}}{(K)}=0, then Colf​(K)={[0,ℓ],[h,k]}{\rm Col}_{f}(K)=\{[0,\ell],[h,k]\}, where ℓ=ColQ0N​(K)\ell={\rm Col}^{N}_{Q_{0}}{(K)}, k=|Q0|k=|Q_{0}|, and h=|Q1|/|Q0|h=|Q_{1}|/|Q_{0}|.

  • •

    If f:Q1→Q0f:Q_{1}\rightarrow Q_{0} has image Q0′Q_{0}^{\prime}, let f′:Q1→Q0′f^{\prime}:Q_{1}\rightarrow Q_{0}^{\prime} be the same map with the codomain Q0′Q_{0}^{\prime}, then Colf​(K)=Colf′​(K)∪{[0,h]}{\rm Col}_{f}(K)={\rm Col}_{f^{\prime}}(K)\cup\{[0,h]\} where hh is the number of colorings by Q0Q_{0} such that some colors are not from Q0′Q_{0}^{\prime}.

  • •

    If f:Q1=Q0×Q0′→Q0f:Q_{1}=Q_{0}\times Q_{0}^{\prime}\rightarrow Q_{0} is the projection from a product quandle, then Colf​(K)={[h,k]}{\rm Col}_{f}(K)=\{[h,k]\}, where k=ColQ0​(K)k={\rm Col}_{Q_{0}}{(K)} and h=ColQ0′​(K)h={\rm Col}_{Q_{0}^{\prime}}{(K)}.

Remark 6.6

For all examples of epimorphisms f:Q1→Q0f:Q_{1}\rightarrow Q_{0} we computed, the invariant Colf​(K){\rm Col}_{f}{(K)} is determined by (ColQ1​(K),ColQ0​(K))({\rm Col}_{Q_{1}}{(K)},{\rm Col}_{Q_{0}}{(K)}). Specifically, for these epimorphisms and all pairs of knots KK and K′K^{\prime} with at most 1212 crossings, if (ColQ1​(K),ColQ0​(K))=(ColQ1​(K′),ColQ0​(K′))({\rm Col}_{Q_{1}}{(K)},{\rm Col}_{Q_{0}}{(K)})=({\rm Col}_{Q_{1}}{(K^{\prime})},{\rm Col}_{Q_{0}}{(K^{\prime})}) then Colf​(K)=Colf​(K′){\rm Col}_{f}{(K)}={\rm Col}_{f}{(K^{\prime})}. This holds for epimorphisms C⁡[6,1]→C⁡[3,1]C[6,1]\rightarrow C[3,1], C⁡[8,1]→C⁡[4,1]C[8,1]\rightarrow C[4,1], and C⁡[9,1]→C⁡[3,1]C[9,1]\rightarrow C[3,1]. It also holds for C⁡[18,5]→C⁡[6,2]C[18,5]\rightarrow C[6,2], for many knots (not necessarily all 29772977 knots) we computed.

Furthermore, for C⁡[6,1]→C⁡[3,1]C[6,1]\rightarrow C[3,1], the invariant is determined by ColC⁡[6,1]​(K){\rm Col}_{C[6,1]}{(K)} alone for many knots, while for C⁡[8,1]→C⁡[4,1]C[8,1]\rightarrow C[4,1] and C⁡[9,1]→C⁡[3,1]C[9,1]\rightarrow C[3,1], both ColQ1​(K){\rm Col}_{Q_{1}}{(K)} and ColQ0​(K){\rm Col}_{Q_{0}}{(K)} are needed to determine the invariant.

Remark 6.7

From the considerations in the preceding remark, it is of interest whether the number of colorings of a quandle determines that of another. There are many such pairs among RIG quandles over all 29772977 knots. We note that many of the pairs do not have epimorphisms between them, and more studies on this phenomenon may be desirable.

Remark 6.8

The quandle 22-cocycle invariant was defined in [6] as follows. Let ϕ:X×X→A\phi:X\times X\rightarrow A be a quandle 22-cocycle, for a finite quandle XX and an abelian group AA. For a knot diagram KK and a coloring x∈SColX​(K)x\in{\rm SCol}_{X}{(K)}, the weight at a crossing τ\tau as depicted in Figure 2 is defined by Bϕ​(τ,x)=ϵ​ϕ​(x,y)B_{\phi}(\tau,x)=\epsilon\phi(x,y), where ϵ=±1\epsilon=\pm 1 is the sign of τ\tau, defined as +1+1 if the under-arc points right in the figure, otherwise −1-1. The 22-cocycle invariant Φϕ​(K)\Phi_{\phi}(K) is defined as the multiset {∑τBϕ​(τ,x)|x∈SColX​(K)}\{\sum_{\tau}B_{\phi}(\tau,x)\ |\ x\in{\rm SCol}_{X}{(K)}\}.

The cocycle invariant and the invariant Colf​(K){\rm Col}_{f}(K), which we defined for an epimorphism f:Q1→Q0f:Q_{1}\rightarrow Q_{0} for quandles QiQ_{i}, i=0,1i=0,1, can be naturally combined as follows. Let AA be an abelian group, and ϕi\phi_{i}, i=0,1i=0,1, be 22-cocycles of QiQ_{i}. Then define Φf;ϕ1,ϕ0​(K)\Phi_{f;\phi_{1},\phi_{0}}(K) to be a multiset

{(∑τBϕ0​(τ,x),{∑τBϕ1​(τ,y)|y∈f♯−1​(x)})|x∈SColQ0​(K)}.\{\ (\sum_{\tau}B_{\phi_{0}}(\tau,x),\ \{\sum_{\tau}B_{\phi_{1}}(\tau,y)\ |\ y\in f_{\sharp}^{-1}(x)\}\ )\ |\ x\in{\rm SCol}_{Q_{0}}{(K)}\}.

7 Applications to other knot invariants

In this section we give applications of the number of quandle colorings to a few invariants for the 2977 knots in [8]. In particular, we determine the tunnel number for some of the knots with 11 and 12 crossings in [8]. For definitions of knot invariants, we refer to [8, 44].

Recall that ColX​(K){\rm Col}_{X}(K) denotes the number of colorings of a knot KK by a finite quandle XX. Let LqX​(K){\rm Lq}_{X}(K) denote ⌈log|X|⁡(ColX​(K))⌉\lceil\log_{|X|}({\rm Col}_{X}(K))\rceil, where |X||X| denotes the order of XX.

We computed LqQ​(K){\rm Lq}_{Q}(K) for the 2977 knots over a set 𝒬ℒ{\cal QL} of 439 quandles consisting of all 431 RIG quandles and the 8 quandles QiQ_{i}, i=16,18,19,20,22,23,25i=16,18,19,20,22,23,25 from the 26 quandles QiQ_{i} in Table B.1. The additional 8 quandles are not Alexander. Let MLq⁡(K){\rm MLq}(K) be the maximum of LqQ​(K){\rm Lq}_{Q}(K) over all of the 439439 quandles in 𝒬ℒ{\cal QL}. Among 29772977 knots with 1212 crossings or less, there are 14731473 knots KK with MLq⁡(K)=2{\rm MLq}(K)=2, 14411441 knots with MLq=3{\rm MLq}=3, and 6363 (1515 11-crossing and 48 12-crossing) knots with MLq=4{\rm MLq}=4. Let MLqF​(K){\rm MLq}^{F}(K) denote the maximum of LqX​(K){\rm Lq}_{X}(K) over all Alexander RIG quandles of the form Λp/(h⁡(t))\Lambda_{p}/(h(t)) where h⁡(t)h(t) is irreducible in ℤp​[t]\mathbb{Z}_{p}[t] for prime pp and different from tt and t−1t-1. Note that MLq{\rm MLq} and MLqF{\rm MLq}^{F} are defined over all quandles in the particular set 𝒬ℒ{\cal QL}. The computational results on these are listed in [49].

Bridge index

Let Bg⁡(K){\rm Bg}(K) denote the bridge index of a knot KK. In [43], a lower bound of the bridge index is given in terms of the number of quandle colorings: Let XX be a finite quandle. For an nn-bridge presentation of a knot, an assignment of colors at the nn maxima determines the colors of the remaining arcs of the diagram, if it extends to the entire diagram and gives a well-defined coloring. Hence we have |ColX​(K)|≤|X|n|{\rm Col}_{X}(K)|\leq|X|^{n}, where |X||X| denotes the order of XX. Thus we obtain LqX​(K)≤Bg⁡(K){\rm Lq}_{X}(K)\leq{\rm Bg}(K), and therefore, MLq⁡(K)≤Bg⁡(K){\rm MLq}(K)\leq{\rm Bg}(K).

It is proved in [3] that a Motesinos knot KK with rr rational tangle summands has Bg⁡(K)=r{\rm Bg}(K)=r. In [35], Montesinos knots were used for determining the bridge indices of knots with 1111 crossings. In particular, the set of 44-bridge 11 crossing knots identified in [35] agreed with the list of 11 crossing knots with MLq=4{\rm MLq}=4. These are:

11​a​¯​43,11​a​¯​44,11​a​¯​47,11​a​¯​57,11​a​¯​231,11​a​¯​263,\displaystyle 11a\underline{\ }43,11a\underline{\ }44,11a\underline{\ }47,11a\underline{\ }57,11a\underline{\ }231,11a\underline{\ }263,
11​n​¯​71,11​n​¯​72,11​n​¯​73,11​n​¯​74,11​n​¯​75,11​n​¯​76,11​n​¯​77,11​n​¯​78,11​n​¯​81.\displaystyle 11n\underline{\ }71,11n\underline{\ }72,11n\underline{\ }73,11n\underline{\ }74,11n\underline{\ }75,11n\underline{\ }76,11n\underline{\ }77,11n\underline{\ }78,11n\underline{\ }81.

At the time of writing, KnotInfo [8] did not have informalion on the bridge index for 12 crossing knots. The set of 1212 crossing Montesinos knots with 44 rational tangle summands were computed by Slavik Jablan using LinKnot [24], and the list was provided to us by Chad Musick. There are 48 knots in their table. Our computation showed that there are 4848 knots with 12 crossings with MLq=4{\rm MLq}=4, and the list can be found in [49]. These two lists coincide.

Nakanishi index

We use the notations Λ=ℤ⁡[t,t−1]\Lambda=\mathbb{Z}[t,t^{-1}] and Λp=ℤp​[t,t−1]\Lambda_{p}=\mathbb{Z}_{p}[t,t^{-1}]. The Nakanishi index NI⁡(K){\rm NI}(K) of a knot KK is the minimum size of square presentation matrices of the Alexander module (H1​(Y~)H_{1}(\tilde{Y}) as a Λ\Lambda-module, where Y~\tilde{Y} is the infinite cyclic covering of the complement YY) of KK [36]. The Nakanishi index for 1111 and 1212 crossing knots was blank in [8] when this project was started (June, 2012). We examine how much of the Nakanishi index can be determined for these knots using quandle colorings.

Lemma 7.1

For any knot KK and Alexander quandle QQ of the form Λp/(h⁡(t))\Lambda_{p}/(h(t)) where h⁡(t)h(t) is irreducible in ℤp​[t]\mathbb{Z}_{p}[t] for prime pp and different from tt and t−1t-1, it holds that

LqQ​(K)≤NI⁡(K)+1≤Bg⁡(K).{\rm Lq}_{Q}(K)\leq{\rm NI}(K)+1\leq{\rm Bg}(K).

Proof. As in the proof of Proposition 5.4, Λp/(h⁡(t))\Lambda_{p}/(h(t)) is a finite field 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} of order qq denoted by 𝔽⁡(p,h⁡(t))\mathbb{F}(p,h(t)) in [2], where q=pkq=p^{k} for a prime pp and k=deg⁡(h⁡(t))k={\rm deg}(h(t)).

It is shown in [2] that if AA is a presentation matrix of the Alexander module, then the same matrix reduced modulo pp, A(p)A^{(p)}, is a presentation matrix of H1​(Y~,ℤp)H_{1}(\tilde{Y};\mathbb{Z}_{p}) as a Λp\Lambda_{p}-module. Let A(p)¯\overline{A^{(p)}} be the matrix A(p)A^{(p)} with entries reduced modulo h⁡(t)h(t).

Let ψ:Λpn→Λpn\psi:\Lambda_{p}^{n}\rightarrow\Lambda_{p}^{n} denote the map corresponding to A(p)A^{(p)}, and ψ¯:𝔽qn→𝔽qn\overline{\psi}:\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n} denote the map on the vector space 𝔽qn\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n} corresponding to A(p)¯\overline{A^{(p)}}. Then in [2] it was shown that the set of colorings SColQ​(K){\rm SCol}_{Q}{(K)} is in one-to-one correspondence with the vector space 𝔽q⊕ker⁡(ψ¯)\mathbb{F}_{q}\oplus{\rm ker}(\overline{\psi}).

If NI⁡(K)=n{\rm NI}(K)=n, then there is an n×nn\times n presentation matrix AA for the Alexander module. Then ker⁡(ψ¯){\rm ker}(\overline{\psi}) has dimension at most nn. Hence

ColQ​(K)=|𝔽q⊕ker⁡(ψ¯)|=q1+dim​ker​(ψ¯)≤q1+n,{\rm Col}_{Q}{(K)}=|\mathbb{F}_{q}\oplus{\rm ker}(\overline{\psi})|=q^{1+{\rm dim\,ker}(\overline{\psi})}\leq q^{1+n},

so that we obtain LqQ​(K)≤1+n{\rm Lq}_{Q}(K)\leq 1+n. It is well known that NI⁡(K)+1≤Bg⁡(K){\rm NI}(K)+1\leq{\rm Bg}(K). □\Box

Corollary 7.2

For any knot KK, MLqF​(K)≤NI⁡(K)+1≤Bg⁡(K){\rm MLq}^{F}(K)\leq{\rm NI}(K)+1\leq{\rm Bg}(K).

For 10 crossing knots, in KnotInfo [8] as of October 2013, the following knots are listed as having NI=2{\rm NI}=2: 10​¯​k10\underline{\ }k for

k=61,63,65,69,74,75,98,99,101,103,122,123,140,142,144,155,157,160.k=61,63,65,69,74,75,98,99,101,103,122,123,140,142,144,155,157,160.

The list of 10 crossing knots such that Corollary 7.2 determines that NI=2{\rm NI}=2 consists of 10​¯​ℓ10\underline{\ }\ell for

ℓ=61,63,65,74,75,98,99,103,115,122,123,140,142,144,155,157,163.\ell=61,63,65,74,75,98,99,103,115,122,123,140,142,144,155,157,163.

Thus Corollary 7.2 determines knots with NI=2{\rm NI}=2 for all but k=k=69, 101, and 160. We point out that Corollary 7.2 implies NI=2{\rm NI}=2 for k=k=115 and 163, these values of NI are posted in [8] incorrectly as having NI=1{\rm NI}=1. This error was corrected in [28] (the knot 1016310_{163} is denoted as 1016410_{164} in [28]).

The 1111 and 1212 crossing knots with MLqF​(K)=3{\rm MLq}^{F}(K)=3, and therefore, NI⁡(K)≥2{\rm NI}(K)\geq 2 by Corollary 7.2, are listed in [49]. Among these, knots with Bg⁡(K)=3{\rm Bg}(K)=3 are determined to have NI⁡(K)=2{\rm NI}(K)=2 by Corollary 7.2. In particular, 11 crossing knots in this list (46 knots) have bridge index 3 by [35], and therefore, have NI=2{\rm NI}=2.

Tunnel number

Let τ⁡(K)\tau(K) denote the tunnel number of a knot KK. At the writing of this article (October 2013), KnotInfo [8] did not contain the tunnel number for knots with 11 or more crossings.

Let QQ be a quandle of the form Λp/(h⁡(t))\Lambda_{p}/(h(t)) for a prime pp and an irreducible polynomial h⁡(t)h(t) as before. It was shown in [23] (see also [2]) that LqQ​(K)≤τ⁡(K)+1{\rm Lq}_{Q}(K)\leq\tau(K)+1 for any knot KK. It is well known that τ⁡(K)+1≤Bg⁡(K)\tau(K)+1\leq{\rm Bg}(K) holds for any knot KK. Hence we obtain the following lemma.

Lemma 7.3

If LqQ​(K)=Bg​(K){\rm Lq}_{Q}(K)={\rm Bg}(K) for some quandle QQ of the form Λp/(h⁡(t))\Lambda_{p}/(h(t)) where h⁡(t)h(t) is irreducible in ℤp​[t]\mathbb{Z}_{p}[t] for prime pp and different from tt and t−1t-1, then τ⁡(K)=Bg⁡(K)−1\tau(K)={\rm Bg}(K)-1.

As we mentioned earlier the bridge index was determined for all 11 crossing knots in [35]. Unknotting number

It is known [36] that the unknotting number u⁡(K)u(K) of a knot KK is bounded below by NI⁡(K){\rm NI}(K): NI⁡(K)≤u⁡(K){\rm NI}(K)\leq u(K). We use this fact to examine the unknotting number of knots in the KnotInfo table.

We consider the knots with MLqF​(K)=3{\rm MLq}^{F}(K)=3. The knots in the table with MLqF​(K)=3{\rm MLq}^{F}(K)=3 are posted at [49], together with the first simple prime power Alexander quandle XX that gives LqX​(K)=3{\rm Lq}_{X}(K)=3. A file containing knots with MLqF​(K)=3{\rm MLq}^{F}(K)=3 and their unknotting numbers is also found at [48]. In the list, the notation [2,3][2,3] means u⁡(K)=2u(K)=2 or 33, which we also denote by u⁡(K)=[2,3]u(K)=[2,3] below for shorthand. Appendix

Appendix A Enumeration of quandles and properties of RIG quandles

Sequences enumerating quandles of order nn with various properties may be found in the Online Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences [42]. We list the OEIS identification numbers of some of these sequences below. We also list below some properties and characterizations of RIG quandles that may be found in files at [48].

  • •

    http://oeis.org/A193024. The number of isomorphism classes of Alexander quandles of order nn.

  • •

    http://oeis.org/A193067. The number of isomorphism classes of connected Alexander quandles of order nn.

  • •

    http://oeis.org/A225744. The number of isomorphism classes of connected Generalized Alexander quandles of order nn.

  • •

    http://oeis.org/A196111 The number of isomorphism classes of simple quandles of order nn. A quandle is simple if it has more than one element, and if it has no homomorphic images other than itself or the singleton quandle. However, in [1], it is further assumed that simple quandles are not trivial. This also rules out the quandles of order 2.

  • •

    http://oeis.org/A177886 The number of isomorphism classes of latin quandles of order nn. A Latin quandle is a quandle such that for each a∈Xa\in X, the left translation ℒa{\cal L}_{a} is a bijection. That is, the multiplication table of the quandle is a Latin square.

  • •

    https://oeis.org/A226172 The number of isomorphism classes of faithful connected quandles of order nn. A quandle is faithful if the mapping a↦ℛaa\mapsto{\cal R}_{a} from XX to Inn⁡(X){\rm Inn}(X) is an injection.

  • •

    https://oeis.org/A226173 The number of isomorphism classes of connected keis (involutory quandles) of order nn. A quandle XX is involutory, or a kei, if the right translations are involutions: ℛa2=id{\cal R}_{a}^{2}={\rm id} for all a∈Xa\in X.

  • •

    https://oeis.org/A226174 The number of isomorphism classes of self-dual connected quandles of order nn.

We also obtained the following information about RIG quandles. This is available at [48]:

  • •

    Subquandles of RIG quandles that are RIG quandles and trivial quandles. We also identified the orders of subquandles that are neither connected nor trivial.

  • •

    The connected RIG Alexander quandles are presented as ℤ⁡[t]/J\mathbb{Z}[t]/J where J=(f⁡(t))J=(f(t)) or J=(f⁡(t),g⁡(t))J=(f(t),g(t)) except for one Alexander RIG quandle, namely C⁡[27,17]C[27,17], which is not a cyclic ℤ⁡[t,t−1]\mathbb{Z}[t,t^{-1}]-module.

  • •

    We identified RIG quandles that are products of other RIG quandles.

  • •

    We identified dual quandles of RIG quandles. In particular, if the dual is itself, then it is self-dual.

  • •

    A function ϕ:X×X→A\phi:X\times X\rightarrow A for an abelian group AA is called a quandle 22-cocycle if it satisfies

    ϕ⁡(x,y)−ϕ⁡(x,z)+ϕ⁡(x∗y,z)−ϕ⁡(x∗z,y∗z)=0\phi(x,y)-\phi(x,z)+\phi(x*y,z)-\phi(x*z,y*z)=0

    and ϕ⁡(x,x)=0\phi(x,x)=0 for any x,y,z∈Xx,y,z\in X. For a quandle 22-cocycle ϕ\phi, X×AX\times A becomes a quandle by (x,a)∗(y,b)=(x∗y,a+ϕ⁡(x,y))(x,a)*(y,b)=(x*y,a+\phi(x,y)) for x,y∈Xx,y\in X, a,b∈Aa,b\in A, and it is called an abelian extension of XX by AA. See [5], for example, for more details of extensions. A list of RIG quandles that are abelian extensions of RIG quandles is found in [48].

  • •

    For each RIG quandle C⁡[n,i]C[n,i] we identified a set Gen[n,i][n,i] which is a smallest set of generators for C⁡[n,i]C[n,i]. We also produced the set of all [n,i][n,i] such that any two elements of C⁡[n,i]C[n,i] will generate C⁡[n,i]C[n,i]. Note that if [n,i][n,i] is in this set then there are no non-trivial subquandles of C⁡[n,i]C[n,i].

Remark A.1

It is known that connected quandles of prime order pp and those of order p2p^{2} are Alexander quandles. By examining characterizations and properties of RIG quandles, listed above, one might wonder if these results might generalize. For example, RIG quandles of order 2n2^{n} for some nn, and those with order p​qpq for primes p,q>3p,q>3 are Alexander. However, inspections of higher order conjugation quandles reveal that there are quandles with order 6464 and 5555 that are not Alexander. The former is a size 64 conjugacy class of GAP’s SmallGroup(1344,11699)(1344,11699). Two of the latter are a conjugacy class of PSL(2,11)(2,11) and a conjugacy class of SmallGroup(1210,7)(1210,7).

Remark A.2

As in [20] and [46], for computational purposes we represent quandles by matrices. The entries of the matrix AA of a quandle of order nn are integers 1,…,n1,\ldots,n and the quandle operation is given by i∗j=Ai,ji*j=A_{i,j}. We note that the quandles in the RIG package are left distributive whereas for knot colorings we prefer right distributive quandles. Hence we have reversed the order of the product in the RIG quandle by taking the transposes of the matrices representing the RIG quandles. In the RIG package the ii-th quandle of order nn is denoted by SmallQuandle(n,i)(n,i), for which we use the notation C⁡[n,i]C[n,i].

Appendix D Remarks on the computation of ColQ​(K){\rm Col}_{Q}{(K)}

We used several techniques to compute ColQ​(K){\rm Col}_{Q}{(K)} for quandles QQ and knots KK. We take for each knot the braid representation given at KnotInfo [8]. We take the braids to be oriented from top to bottom. This induces an orientation of the knots. The two parameters that are most important for computing the number of colorings are the braid index, b⁡(K)b(K) (the number of strands) and the order |Q||Q| of the quandle. A straightforward computation requires |Q|b⁡(K)|Q|^{b(K)} steps. Using the fact that our quandles are connected, i.e., the group I​n​n​(Q)Inn(Q) acts transitively on QQ we may assume that one of the arcs has a fixed color. This allowed us to reduce the number of steps to |Q|b⁡(K)−1|Q|^{b(K)-1}, which reduces the time by a factor of 1/|Q|1/|Q|. In the case of quandles of large order this makes a noticeable difference in program running times (hours vs months).

We initially used Mace4 [33] to find the number of colorings. Later on, we wrote a program in C to verify that the results we obtained using Mace4 were correct. The C program uses the same braid representations as those used for the Mace4 computations.

Let KK be a knot with a braid index b⁡(K)b(K). Let QQ be a quandle of order nn. Let aia_{i}, i=1,…,bi=1,\ldots,b, represent the element of a given quandle assigned to the top of the ii-th strand of a braid, where b=b⁡(K)b=b(K) is the braid index. To count the number of knot colorings, we find the colorings at the bottom strands of the braid, and check assignments such that the top and bottom colors are the same for each strand, compare Figure 2. The following pseudo code demonstrates that our algorithm runs in O⁡(nb−1)O(n^{b-1}) time, n=|Q|n=|Q|.

⬇
/* fix strand a1 to be 0. This allows us to get away *
* with coloring b-1 strands instead of b strands. */
a1=0;
for(a2=0; a2 < n; a2++) {
for(a3 …) {
for(a4 …) {
for(a5 …) {
… up to the braid index ’b’
/* constant time quandle coloring of knot strands */
}
}
}
}

We implemented a multithreaded version of the program using POSIX threads to further improve performance. Combined with fixing a color of one strand, we found that multithreading reduces the computation time considerably on multicore processors. The unexpectedly large speedup of multithreading over trivial parallelization may be due to operating system characteristics and prevention of CPU cache swapping to the slower RAM when the operating system is switching tasks.

The computations were performed on a GNU/Linux computer equipped with 24 Gigabytes of RAM and an Intel Core i7 processor with 4 cores. The kernel was compiled with a task switching latency of 100hz.

In Table 1, the first column indicates 2626 quandles in Table B.1, the second column gives the order of the quandle, the third column is the computation time for all 2977 knots with at most 12 crossings using a single thread, the fourth column is time using multiple threads, and the last column is the ratio of column 33 and column 44. A log plot of timings of three different coloring programs is given in Figure 3.

Multithreading was used to perform computations in parallel for the outermost loop of our knot coloring program. We set the number of threads to be the order of the quandle. None of the child threads communicate with each other. The parent thread waits for all of the child threads to return the number of colorings from its search. The parent sums each of the results from the child threads. The number of colorings of the knot is the sum of the counts from the child threads. The multithreaded version of the program is required to compute the colorings by the quandle of order 182.

⬇
/* fix strand a1 to be 0. This allows us to get away *
* with coloring b-1 strands instead of b strands. */
a1=0;
/* when multithreading, we compute b-2 strands since a2 is fixed */
a2=thread_id;
/* for each thread */
for(a3=0; a3 < n; a3++) {
for(a4 …) {
for(a5 …) {
… up to the braid index ’b’
/* constant time quandle coloring of knot strands */
}
}
}

The output of our program is the number ColQ​(K)0{\rm Col}_{Q}(K)_{0} of colorings with the color of the first strand fixed. The result is then converted to the number of non-trivial colorings ColQN​(K){\rm Col}^{N}_{Q}(K) using the formula ColQN​(K)=|Q|​(ColQ​(K)0−1){\rm Col}^{N}_{Q}(K)=|Q|({\rm Col}_{Q}(K)_{0}-1).

All of the programs we used are provided on-line at [48] with source and data sets available. We made numerous checks, but would be pleased if our computations can be independently confirmed.
